new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prosody is a culminative high-pitch (tone / 'pitch-accent') system, not stress: each word has exactly one high-pitched syllable; by default (about 80% of words) it is the word-final syllable, but its position is lexically and grammatically contrastive (kóma vs koma, tóba vs toba), so non-final accent must be marked. The accented syllable carries no extra length or intensity; word-final syllables are in fact the shortest and a final high vowel may drop in connected speech, the word's final accent then being signalled only by the absence of high pitch elsewhere. Merlan & Rumsey 1991:324 labelled this 'pitch-accent'; Rumsey 2007/2010 prefers to call it a (restricted) tone system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the system is stated to assign a pitch peak to just one syllable per word, and no strong/weak distinction among other syllables plays any role (Rumsey 2010: 47).
new_statements.exceptions: ~20% of polysyllabic words have the peak on a non-final syllable (lexically specified, marked with acute in the orthography); a handful of monosyllables with phonetically long (bimoraic) vowels, e.g. naá 'not' vs na 'I', carry the high tone on the second mora; in connected speech a final open high-vowel syllable may be elided, leaving no surface high-toned syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about words 'pronounced carefully in isolation' (citation forms); Rumsey notes final-syllable shortening/elision in connected speech and that the sung tom yaya melody largely overrides lexical tone. Described variety is the Ku Waru dialect of Bo-Ung.
new_statements.identity_note: All accessible descriptions are of Ku Waru ('Steep Stone'), the westernmost dialect area of Bo-Ung/Mbo-Ung [mux], straddling the Tambul Range on the western edge of the Nebilyer Valley (Rumsey 2010: 39). Glottolog 5.1 attaches Merlan & Rumsey 1991 (Ku Waru) to boun1245 but lists only Mara-Gomu (mara1405) and Miyemu (miye1238) as dialect nodes; Ku Waru has no separate glottocode. Rumsey explicitly rejects a stress analysis: the system is culminative lexical high pitch (default word-final), labelled 'pitch-accent' in Merlan & Rumsey 1991 and 'tone' in Rumsey 2007/2010 -- catalog entry should be coded pitch-accent/tonal rather than fixed-final stress.

sources.note: Sec. 3 'Aspects of Ku Waru segmental phonology and prosody', pp. 43-44: every polysyllabic word has exactly one syllable with a pitch peak; for ~80% of words it is the final syllable; position is lexically/grammatically contrastive (koma 'carry on shoulder' vs kóma 'wet'; toba FUT vs tóba NF); explicitly NOT a stress-accent system -- high-pitched syllables are not longer or louder, final syllables are the shortest and high final vowels often drop in connected speech; p. 47: no strong/weak syllable distinction plays any role within words.

sources.citation: Rumsey, Alan & Don Niles (eds). 2011. Sung Tales from the Papua New Guinea Highlands: Studies in Form, Meaning, and Sociocultural Context. Canberra: ANU E Press. (ch. 11 Rumsey 'Style, plot, and character in Tom Yaya tales from Ku Waru'; ch. 12 Niles on Hagen-area metric melodies)
sources.note: Ch. 11 pp. 255, 258 fn. 15: Ku Waru sung metre 'is based not on a distinction between strong and weak syllables, but on syllable timing and word boundaries'; Ku Waru has great variability of syllable length and is not 'syllable-timed'; refers to Rumsey 2010 for phonetic details. No word-stress placement rule stated.

sources.citation: Rumsey, Alan. 2007. Musical, poetic, and linguistic form in Tom Yaya sung narratives from Papua New Guinea. Anthropological Linguistics 49(3/4): 235-282.
sources.note: pp. 237-238: same statement as 2010 (single pitch-peak syllable per word, ~80% word-final, contrastive pairs koma/kóma, toba/tóba; unlike stress-accent languages the peak syllable is not longer or higher-energy). Fn. 4 (p. 272): Merlan & Rumsey 1991:324 called this a 'pitch-accent' system; following Hyman 2006 Rumsey now avoids that label and speaks of the Ku Waru tone system. Fn. 5: monosyllables all have the same early-peak falling pattern except a few bimoraic words (naá 'not').
